h1:
Fisherman's Village, Bophut
Seafood, cafes & old wooden shophouses by the sea
intro: Bophut Fisherman's Village, known to most visitors simply as Fisherman's Village, is an old quarter on the north side of Koh Samui, right by Bophut Beach. Its charm is the narrow main lane lined with wooden shophouses and Chinese-style row houses that have stood for over a hundred years. Today the ground floors are seafood restaurants, cafes, beach bars, and souvenir shops all mixed together. We'll walk you through it corner by corner, from toes-in-the-sand seafood to morning coffee in an old timber house, with notes on the area layout, rough prices, and when the walking street market runs.

blocks.html: Bophut is different from Chaweng or Lamai in that it still has an old, story-telling feel. The village's main street runs less than a kilometre, so it's an easy stroll, with timber row houses and Chinese masonry buildings on both sides where older Samui families have lived since this really was a fishing village. These days the ground floors are open as shops, but the building frames, folding wooden doors, and old signs are still there, which makes eating and photographing your way through here more enjoyable than a typical beach strip.

Bophut sits close to Samui Airport and the piers for Koh Phangan and Koh Tao, about a 10–15 minute drive from Chaweng, so a lot of people stop here for dinner before or after a flight. Parking in the village is limited, so if you come on a market evening, allow extra time to find a spot on the outskirts and walk in.

Bophut's standout draw is the restaurants right on the beach, where they set tables down on the sand. In the late afternoon, once the heat drops and the breeze picks up, you can sit over prawns, clams, crab, and fish while the sun sets over toward Koh Phangan. We've picked the places people actually go to based on real reviews, ranked by popularity and value for the price — though whose cooking suits your taste is personal, so use location and budget as your main guide.

items.name: Krua Bophut
items.blurb: A long-running Thai–seafood restaurant in the village, with both an indoor section and tables out on Bophut Beach itself. The strength here is genuine Thai food — tom yum, stir-fried curries, steamed fish. The mood is relaxed, and you can catch the sunset in the evening. It's the place most people think of first when it comes to beachfront dining in Bophut.
items.price: THB 150–400 per dish · fresh fish/prawns by the kilo

items.name: La Brisa
items.blurb: A beachfront Thai–seafood restaurant that sets tables out on the sand after 5pm. People like it for the chilled vibe before it gets crowded. The most-ordered dish is the big mixed seafood platter — great for sharing if you come as a group.

items.name: The FishHouse Restaurant & Bar
items.blurb: A seafood and international restaurant in the village, focused on grilled fish and shellfish. The space is comfortable to sit in and there's a bar on-site, so it works for a dinner where you want both seafood and drinks in one spot.

items.name: Red Snapper Restaurant & Bar
items.blurb: A Western-style restaurant and bar with a seafood streak, plus live music on some nights. People come to settle in for a long dinner that carries on over drinks. The menu has fish, steaks, and small plates — good for couples who want a bit of music with the meal.

items.name: 2 Fishes
items.blurb: A beachfront spot known for handmade Italian food paired with fresh fish. The pasta and fish here are well done, the prices lean premium, and it suits a special meal by the sea. Usually closed Mondays — worth calling to book ahead.

items.name: Gusto Italiano & Bistro
items.blurb: A beachfront Italian run by an Italian couple, known for wood-fired pizza and handmade pasta. There's an early-evening aperitivo from 5 to 7pm. Good for anyone wanting a break from Thai seafood with something European by the sea.

items.name: Charm
items.blurb: A small, family-run Asian fusion spot with a friendly mood and 80s music playing. The menu is Thai–Asian with a modern twist, mains are mid-range, and it's a good pick for a casual, easygoing meal in the village.

items.name: The Shack Grill
items.blurb: A long-standing steakhouse in the area, open for more than 20 years, known for hand-cut Australian Angus beef grilled fresh, plus sushi-grade tuna and lobster. Good for meat lovers who want a proper meal — book early in the evening.

blocks.title: Read this before ordering fresh catch
blocks.html: Prices for seafood sold by the kilo — lobster, crab, large clams — rise and fall with the season and the monsoon. The prices we've listed are rough ranges from reviews. When you're there, ask the price per kilo or per dish before ordering anything weighed fresh, so there are no surprises at the bill. Many beachfront places only set tables down on the sand in the evening, so if you're set on a sand-side table, it's worth asking the timing first.

blocks.text: Cafes and coffee shops in old wooden shophouses

blocks.html: Another part of Bophut's charm is the cafes set up in the old row houses — a coffee-and-bakery shop on the ground floor with the original timber frame and walls still in place, and some looking out to the sea. They're good for breakfast or a midday break before you carry on.

items.name: Bar Baguette
items.blurb: A coffee-and-bakery in the village with house-baked bread and croissants and a view out to the sea. People like settling in for breakfast over coffee, watching the world go by.

items.name: Beach Coconut Bowls
items.blurb: A healthy spot serving fruit bowls, wholegrain bread, and clean breakfasts with a beach-chic mood — good if you want to start the day light.

items.name: Greenlight Café & Bar
items.blurb: A cafe with organic ingredients and good smoothies, plus a yoga studio on-site — good for the wellness crowd who want to linger.

items.name: Café K.O.B Bophut
items.blurb: A coffee shop pairing coffee with filling, easy-on-the-wallet dishes in a simple, casual style — good for a budget lunch.

blocks.html: Bophut Beach faces north–east, so the evening light is lovely and the surf is gentle — a good place to sit and watch the sun slip down over toward Koh Phangan. The beach bars here are where people gather to end the day with a drink, toes in the sand.

items.name: Coco Tam's
items.blurb: The best-known beach bar in Bophut, with cushions on the sand, swing seats at the bar, and a fire show every night (around 19:30 and 21:00). The mood is great but drinks lean pricey, and the beachfront section takes cash. Come around sunset to get a good seat.
items.price: Cocktails THB 250–400 · sand section cash only

items.name: Rice x De Pier
items.blurb: A glass-fronted restaurant-bar on the water with an open view, running long hours from 9am to 11pm. There's risotto, pizza, and fish carpaccio — good if you want the view, the food, and the drinks all in one place.

blocks.title: On the sea and staying safe
blocks.html: During the monsoon (roughly October–December), the Bophut side can get wind, waves, and rain in spells, and some days the sand-side tables get packed up early. Before planning a long stretch on the beach, check that day's forecast. If you're going to swim or take a boat on to a nearby island, judge the sea conditions and follow the operator's announcements first — safety before anything else.

Bophut's highlight for street-food lovers is the walking street, when the village's main road is closed off for a night market with food, souvenirs, clothes, and live music. You graze your way along it under the old wooden shophouses strung with lights.

items: When it runs — Friday night is the main market and the best known, roughly 17:00–23:00. In some seasons there are extra Monday and Wednesday nights too. Days can shift with the season, so check with your hotel or the village page before you go.
Best time to go — 18:00–20:00, when it's not as packed as later and stalls are still fully stocked, so it's easy to walk.
Popular eats — mango sticky rice, prawn pad thai, grilled seafood, pork ribs, and cocktails in the low hundreds of baht. Street-food prices start in the tens to low hundreds of baht.
Entry fee — none, it's free to walk in; it's an open street market.
What to bring — cash, since many street-food stalls still don't take transfers, and parking is scarce, so come early or park on the outskirts and walk in.

blocks.text: Planning a half-day of eating in Bophut

blocks.html: If you want to cover Bophut fully — the food, the cafes, and the sunset — an afternoon-into-evening on a market day is the best value. Here's a rough guide you can adjust to your own pace.

items.activity: Walk the village's main street, looking at the old wooden buildings and Chinese row houses, and take photos.
items.note: The heat is starting to ease — easier walking than midday.

items.activity: Take a break at a cafe in an old wooden house, over coffee or a snack — Bar Baguette or Café K.O.B, for example.
items.note: Sea-view spots fill up in the evening, so come early for a good seat.

items.activity: Browse the souvenir and craft shops in the village.
items.note: Prices are negotiable — compare a few shops.

items.activity: Head down to Bophut Beach and grab a beach-bar seat for the sunset — Coco Tam's or Rice x De Pier, for example.
items.note: Some bars' sand sections take cash, so have some ready.

items.activity: Toes-in-the-sand seafood dinner — pick a beachfront place like Krua Bophut or La Brisa.
items.note: Ask the price on anything sold by the kilo before ordering.

items.activity: Walk the walking street market (mainly Friday nights) and graze on whatever street food's left.
items.note: Check the market day first — if it doesn't line up, carry on at a bar instead.

faq.q: Where is Bophut Fisherman's Village on Koh Samui?
faq.a: It's on the north side of the island, right by Bophut Beach, about a 10–15 minute drive from the Chaweng area, and close to Samui Airport and the piers for Koh Phangan and Koh Tao. It's an old Chinese row-house quarter that's now full of restaurants, cafes, and beachfront bars.

faq.q: What days is the Bophut walking street market on?
faq.a: The main, best-known market is Friday night, roughly 17:00–23:00. In some seasons there are extra Monday and Wednesday nights too. There's no entry fee — it's free to walk in — but the days can shift with the season, so check with your hotel or the village page before you go. The most comfortable time to walk is 18:00–20:00.

faq.q: Which beachfront seafood spots in Bophut are good, and roughly how much?
faq.a: Places people actually go to that set tables on the sand include Krua Bophut and La Brisa, with single dishes around THB 150–400. Fresh items sold by the kilo, like lobster or crab, rise and fall with the season, so ask the price per kilo before ordering.

faq.q: Are there relaxed cafes in Bophut?
faq.a: Yes — several are set up in old wooden row houses, like Bar Baguette (strong on coffee and bakery), Beach Coconut Bowls (the healthy option), and Café K.O.B (easy on the wallet). They're good for breakfast or a midday break before you carry on.

faq.q: What should I watch out for in Bophut?
faq.a: Parking in the village is scarce, especially on market nights, so come early or park on the outskirts and walk in. Bring cash, since many street-food stalls still don't take transfers. And during the monsoon, roughly October–December, check the forecast before planning a long stretch on the beach.
